content: NME4, also known as Non-metastatic cells 4, is a protein in humans encoded by the NME4 gene. This protein belongs to a family of ubiquitous enzymes that catalyze the transfer of gamma-phosphates between nucleoside and deoxynucleoside triand diphosphates through a phosphohistidine intermediate. These enzymes are products of the nm23 gene family, which includes NME4. The first gene in this family, nm23-H1 (also referred to as NME1), was initially identified due to its reduced expression in a highly metastatic murine melanoma cell line. It was proposed to function as a metastasis-suppressing gene. The human equivalent of this gene was discovered through cDNA library screening using the murine gene as a probe and was found to be homologous to the Drosophila awd gene. Subsequently, a second human gene, nm23-H2 (NME2), was isolated. This gene encodes a protein that shares 88% sequence identity with nm23-H1. The gene products of nm23-H1 and nm23-H2 were previously identified as the A and B subunits of nucleoside diphosphate (NDP) kinases. In mammals, functional NDP kinases are heterohexamers composed of A and B monomers, which can combine in variable ratios to form different hybrid types. These enzymes are expressed at significantly higher levels in tumors compared to normal tissues. In certain cell lines and solid tumors, decreased expression of NME1 is associated with increased metastatic potential. Furthermore, when NME1 is transfected into highly aggressive cell lines, such as human breast carcinoma cells, it reduces their metastatic potential. A third human gene, DR-nm23 (NME3), was identified and found to share high sequence similarity with NME1 and NME2. NME3 is highly expressed during the blast crisis phase of chronic myeloid leukemia. When overexpressed via transfection, NME3 suppresses granulocyte differentiation and induces apoptosis in myeloid precursor cells. Model organisms have been utilized to study the function of NME4. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Nme4tm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi, was generated at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute. Both male and female mice underwent a standardized phenotypic screen to assess the effects of NME4 gene deletion.
